text: For my own part I would wish death to overtake me occupied with nothing but the care of my will, trying to make it calm, unhindered, unconstrained, free.
plain: If death is coming either way, let it find you working on your own character.

text: Go to your mother then; for you deserve to be ill, with her to hold your head.
plain: If you want comfort over growth, go get comforted. Just don't call it a reason to quit.

text: Is it nothing (do you think?) never to accuse any one, God or man, never to blame any, to go in and out with the same countenance?
plain: Never blaming anyone and keeping the same face in good and bad days is the hard thing.

text: 'Take my lands, if you will: take my servants, take my office, take my poor body, yet you will not make me fail to get what I will or fall into what I will to avoid.'
plain: They can take everything outside you. They can't take how you choose to respond.

text: What is our nature? To be free, noble, self-respecting.
plain: You were built to stand on your own and respect yourself. Act like it.

text: No harm but that of failing to do your duty: you will destroy the trustworthy, self-respecting, well-behaved man in you. Look not for any greater harm than this!
plain: The only real damage is letting the better version of yourself die.

text: You think so. So does he, and so do madmen. Opinion is a bad criterion.
plain: Feeling certain proves nothing. Everyone feels right, including fools.

text: You need what you have not got—tranquillity, a mind in accord with Nature, and free from perturbation.
plain: What you're missing isn't more stuff. It's a calm mind.

text: I am richer than you: I am not in an agony as to what Caesar will think of me: I do not flatter any one for that.
plain: Not needing anyone's approval is real wealth.

text: To you all that you have appears small: to me all I have appears great. Your desire can never be fulfilled, mine is fulfilled already.
plain: Wanting more never ends. Being satisfied is the only way to finish.

text: So I say to you, 'Let your desire go.' Do not crave much, and you will obtain.
plain: Grab less and you keep more. Clenching a fist full of things traps your hand.

text: What ought one to say then as each hardship comes? 'I was practising for this, I was training for this.'
plain: When it gets hard, tell yourself this is what the training was for.

text: If now is the time for fever, take your fever in the right way; if for thirst, thirst in the right way, if for hunger, hunger aright.
plain: You can't skip the discomfort, but you control how you carry it.

text: For fever too is a part of life, like walking, sailing, travelling.
plain: Pain and sickness are just part of living, not an interruption of it.

text: Is the world going to be turned upside down by your death?
plain: The world will be fine without you. Relax your grip on the drama.

text: This is my part, that is another's: this no one can hinder, that is subject to hindrance.
plain: Do your part. What other people do is theirs, and they can mess it up.

text: 'My brother ought not to have behaved so to me.' No, but it is his business to look to that; however he may behave, I will deal with him as I ought.
plain: How others behave is on them. How you respond is on you.

text: I am inclined to pleasure: in order to train myself I will incline beyond measure in the opposite direction.
plain: If you lean toward comfort, deliberately lean hard the other way.

text: But to begin with, fly far from enemies that are stronger than you.
plain: Early on, stay away from the temptations you can't beat yet.

text: Man, if it is to your profit to drink it, drink; if not, your conduct is absurd.
plain: Do the hard habit because it helps you, not so you can announce it.

text: But nevertheless a man must prepare himself for solitude too—he must be able to suffice for himself, and able to commune with himself.
plain: Learn to be good company for yourself.

text: Fool, he murders not you, but your paltry body.
plain: The worst anyone can do is take your body. They can't touch you.

text: Great power is always dangerous in a beginner.
plain: Ease into it. Big power before big discipline blows up on you.

text: Take scant food, drink water: refrain from willing to get anything for a while, that you may one day direct your will rationally.
plain: Go without for a while so your wants stop running you.

text: Have you stirred yourself up first? You want to benefit them; then show them in your own life what sort of men philosophy makes, and cease to talk folly.
plain: Don't preach it. Live it first and let them see.

text: Man, if you are worth anything, you must walk alone, and talk to yourself and not hide in the chorus.
plain: If you're worth anything you can stand alone and think for yourself.

text: Learn to bear mockery, look about you, examine yourself, that you may get to know who you are.
plain: Let people laugh and look at yourself honestly. That's how you find out who you are.

text: You must be under discipline, eat to order, touch no sweets, train under compulsion, at a fixed hour, in heat and cold, drink no cold water, nor wine, except to order; you must hand yourself over completely to your trainer as you would to a physician.
plain: Winning means a rigid routine and handing yourself over to the process.

text: Man, consider first, what it is you are undertaking: then consider your own powers, and what you can bear.
plain: Know the job, then know what you can really carry.

text: The man who mixes with other people a good deal either for talk or for a wine-party or generally for social purposes, must needs either grow like them himself or convert them to his likeness; for if you put a quenched coal by one that is burning, either it will put the burning 'one out, or will catch fire from it.
plain: You become the people you hang around, unless you're stronger than they are.

text: Adopt new habits: fix your opinions, exercise yourselves in them.
plain: Change your habits on purpose and drill the new ones.

text: Is it not better to be self-respecting than to be rich?'
plain: Being self-respecting beats being rich.

text: Your evil is to defend yourself badly: that is the only thing you need be careful about.
plain: Your only real failure is defending yourself badly. How they judge you is out of your hands.

text: To use health well is good, to use it ill is evil.
plain: Health and money are neutral. What you do with them decides if they're good.

text: I adjure you by the gods, cease to admire material things, cease to make yourselves slaves, first of things, and next, for their sake, of men who can acquire them or take them away.
plain: Chase stuff and you end up owned by it and by whoever controls it.

text: So my reviler helps to train me for the contest: he trains me to be patient, dispassionate, gentle.
plain: The person who disrespects you is free reps in patience.

text: We carry these views to the lecture-room door, but no one takes them home: as soon as we leave here we are at war with our slave-boy, with our neighbours, with those who jeer and laugh at us.
plain: Everyone agrees with the wisdom until the first person annoys them.

text: The carpenter does not come and say, 'Hear me discourse on carpentry', but he undertakes a contract and builds a house and so shows that he has acquired the art.
plain: Don't talk about it. Build the thing.

text: Exile? Can one be sent into exile beyond the Universe? One cannot.
plain: You can't actually be cast out of the world. Wherever you are, you're home.

text: You go all that way to Olympia to see athletes killed or matched in battle, and yet have you no wish to see a battle between fever and a man?'
plain: Your own struggle is worth watching. Fight it like it matters.

text: Man, it is an Olympic contest you are about to enter your name for, not a miserable, make-believe match.
plain: This is the real thing. Treat it that way before you sign up.

text: First say to yourself, what manner of man you want to be; when you have settled this, act upon it in all you do; for in pretty nearly all pursuits we see that done.
plain: Decide who you want to be, then act like him in everything.

text: Do you wish to do men good or to receive compliments?
plain: Be honest about whether you're doing this to help or to be praised.

text: The philosopher's school, sirs, is a physician's consulting-room. You must leave it in pain, not in pleasure; for you come to it in disorder, one with a shoulder put out, another with an ulcer, another with fistula, another with headache.
plain: Real learning should sting. If you leave feeling good and unchanged, nothing happened.

text: Rufus was wont to say, 'If you find leisure to praise me, my words are spoken in vain.'
plain: If the audience is busy clapping, the message didn't land.

text: What ill can happen to you in a place where you are not?
plain: Don't suffer over things happening somewhere you aren't.

text: Is it not enough that you should be miserable where you are yourself? Must you needs be miserable overseas, and by letter?
plain: Being upset about your own life is enough. Stop borrowing worry from far away.

text: Do you not know that life is a soldier's service?
plain: Life hands out hard assignments. Take yours without whining.

text: Now to desire what is impossible is slavish and silly; it is to make oneself a stranger in the world, and to fight against God with one's own judgements, as alone one can.
plain: Wanting what can't be is a losing fight against how things are.

text: Do you not know that a good man does nothing for the sake of what men think, but only for the sake of doing right?
plain: Good people do right because it's right, not for how it looks.

text: Will you then never cease to be a babe? Do you not know that he who acts like a child is ridiculous in proportion to his years?
plain: At some point you have to grow up. The older you get, the worse it looks.

text: So too if you long for your son or your friend, when it is not given you to have him, know that you are longing for a fig in winter time.
plain: Missing something that isn't in season anymore is wanting fruit in winter.

text: What harm is there in whispering to yourself as you kiss your child, 'To-morrow you will die', and to your friend in like manner, 'To-morrow you or I shall go away, and we shall see one another no more'?
plain: Remember the people you love won't last. It makes you love them better.

text: Going abroad is a slight change; death is a greater change—from what now is, not to what is not, but to what is not now.
plain: Death is just a bigger move, from what is now to what isn't yet.

text: You will not be, but something else will be, of which the world now has need; for indeed you came into being, not when you willed it, but when the world had need.
plain: You showed up when you were needed. When that's done, something else takes your place.

text: Only make no display of your office, and boast not yourself in it, but prove it by your conduct; be content, even if no one observes you, to live in true health and happiness.
plain: Don't show off. Live well even if nobody's watching.

text: At once you may recover yourself, and pull yourself together, and renew the struggle with the same energy as before; and if you grow faint again, you may renew it again, and if you once attain to victory you are as one who has never failed.
plain: You can restart right now, as many times as it takes. One win erases the failures.

text: Did you not feed this habit, by putting before it acts which were congenial to it?
plain: You feed a bad habit every time you hand it what it likes.

text: And when did a runaway slave ever die of hunger?
plain: People with nothing find a way to eat. You'll be okay too.

text: Will you realize once for all that it is not death that is the source of all man's evils, and of a mean and cowardly spirit, but rather the fear of death?
plain: It's not death that ruins people. It's being scared of it.
